title: 狱中题壁
author: 谭嗣同
intro: Written on a cell wall by a reformer waiting to be executed. He hopes his comrades who fled will survive, then faces death laughing at the sky. Its third line is one of the most heroic in Chinese.
analysis: 1898年，清朝的“戊戌变法”失败，谭嗣同本来有机会逃走，但他决定留下来，说变法需要有人流血。这首诗是他在狱中写在墙上的。前两句用了两个东汉的典故（古代的故事）：张俭被朝廷追捕，逃亡时人们看到门就去投宿，冒险收留他；杜根被太后下令打死，却忍住装死，活了下来，后来重新被重用。谭嗣同用这两个人，希望逃走的同伴能像他们一样得到保护、忍辱活下去，将来继续事业。第三句“我自横刀向天笑”写自己：面对屠刀，仰天大笑，毫不害怕。最后一句“去留肝胆两昆仑”意思是：走的人和留下的人，都是肝胆相照的英雄，都像昆仑山一样高大。（这一句的具体所指，学者有不同理解。）全诗悲壮而豪迈，是中国最有名的绝命诗之一。
analysisEn: In 1898 the Hundred Days’ Reform, an attempt to modernise the Qing government, was crushed. Tan Sitong could have escaped, but he chose to stay, saying that no reform in history had succeeded without someone shedding blood. He wrote this poem on the wall of his prison cell. The first couplet uses two stories from the Eastern Han dynasty. Zhang Jian, hunted by the court, fled from door to door, and families risked their lives to take him in. Du Gen was ordered beaten to death by the empress dowager but played dead, survived, and was later restored to office. By naming them, Tan hopes his comrades who fled will be sheltered like Zhang Jian and endure like Du Gen, living on to carry the cause forward. The third line is about himself: “I lift my blade sideways and laugh at the sky” — facing death without fear. The last line says that those who left and those who stayed are all people of true courage, as great as the Kunlun Mountains. Exactly whom the “two Kunluns” refers to has been debated, but the spirit is clear. The poem is tragic and proud at once, and is among the most famous last poems in Chinese.
background: Tan Sitong (1865–1898) was one of the leaders of the Hundred Days’ Reform. When the Empress Dowager Cixi ended the reform, he refused to flee and was executed with five others — remembered as the “Six Gentlemen of the Hundred Days”. He was 33.
pronunciation: 投止 tóu zhǐ；张俭 jiǎn；须臾 xū yú；横刀 héng；昆仑 kūn lún。
version: 采用通行教材版本。此诗经梁启超等人记录流传，原壁已不存，传本有个别异文，网站用最通行的一种。

lines.py: wàng mén tóu zhǐ sī zhāng jiǎn
lines.lit: Seeing a door, seeking shelter — I think of Zhang Jian;
lines.en: I think of Zhang Jian, sheltered at any door he came to,

lines.py: rěn sǐ xū yú dài dù gēn
lines.lit: enduring death a moment — waiting like Du Gen.
lines.en: and of Du Gen, who held on at death’s edge and lived to return.

lines.py: wǒ zì héng dāo xiàng tiān xiào
lines.lit: I myself hold my sword crosswise and laugh toward the sky;
lines.en: As for me, I raise my blade and laugh at the sky:

lines.py: qù liú gān dǎn liǎng kūn lún
lines.lit: going or staying, liver and gall — two Kunlun mountains.
lines.en: those who left and those who stayed — both stand brave and tall as Kunlun.

words.en: to seek shelter at any door one sees (while fleeing)
words.note: 投止：投宿。今天也作成语，形容逃难时的窘迫。

words.en: Zhang Jian, an Eastern Han official who fled persecution
words.note: 东汉人，逃亡时很多人家冒死收留他。

words.en: to endure (rather than die); to hold on at death’s edge

words.note: 书面语，现代汉语说“一会儿”“片刻”。

words.en: Du Gen, an Eastern Han official who survived by playing dead
words.note: 东汉人，被打后装死逃过一劫。

words.en: to hold a sword crosswise — fearless, ready to fight
liver and gall — courage, loyalty, sincerity
words.note: 今天仍说“肝胆相照”，指真心相待。

words.en: the Kunlun Mountains, symbol of height and greatness
words.note: 中国西部的大山，在神话里也很重要。

imagery.name: 山
imagery.zh: 昆仑山高大雄伟，比喻无论去留都是顶天立地的英雄。
imagery.en: The towering Kunlun Mountains: whether they left or stayed, all were heroes of that stature.
